# Community Is a Job, Not a Number

Source: https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A community earns its keep by doing work the company would otherwise pay for: testing, teaching, referring, building or governing. Decide the job first, design the channel, rituals and recognition around it, and measure contribution to that job instead of member count, which most community teams still lead with.

A community earns its keep by doing work the company would otherwise pay for. Decide the job first, design the community around it, and measure contribution instead of size. Member count is the most common health measure in the field, used by 84% of community teams in CMX's 2025 survey, and it is also the easiest number to inflate and the hardest for anyone outside to verify.

This piece sits at the start of our [complete guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/). The argument is simple. A community is a group of people doing a job together, and the job is what makes it worth the cost.

## Why member count misleads

Member counts are easy to buy, easy to inflate with incentives and nearly impossible for an outsider to verify. Investors know this. Customers do not care. The only person a big number reliably impresses is the founder.

The field still leads with it. CMX's 2025 Community Industry Report, a survey of 589 community professionals, found the number of active members was the most used health metric, at 84%. Only 24% said they could confidently put a financial value on their community, up from 16% the year before. Difficulty proving return on investment was the most cited budget problem, at 37%. A team that reports headcount and cannot show value is reporting the one number that does not answer the budget question.

Counts also hide how participation actually works. Jakob Nielsen's 2006 analysis of participation inequality described the 90-9-1 pattern: in most online communities about 90% of people read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. A 2014 observational study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research tested this across four digital health networks with 63,990 members. The top 1% wrote 74.7% of all posts, the next 9% wrote 24.0% and the remaining 90% wrote 1.3%. Doubling membership mostly doubles the readers.

Incentive-driven growth adds platform risk. On 15 January 2026, X's product lead announced that X had revoked API access for apps that paid users to post, citing "AI slop & reply spam". The Block reported that the KAITO token, tied to the best known of these programmes, fell more than 10% within minutes and was down 14.5% at publication. Kaito said it would wind down its incentivised leaderboards. Any community strategy that depends on one platform's API can be switched off by that platform.

## The five jobs

| Job | What the community does | What you measure | Fits best |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test | Uses early builds, reports bugs, gives feedback | Bugs found, feedback sessions, release sign-offs | Pre-launch products, AI tools |
| Teach | Answers questions, writes guides, onboards newcomers | Share of questions answered by members, guides written | Developer tools, complex DeFi |
| Refer | Brings customers, partners or hires | Referred sign-ups and their conversion | B2B AI, infrastructure |
| Build | Integrates, extends, ships on top of you | Integrations, plugins, forks used | Protocols, platforms, APIs |
| Govern | Makes real decisions with real consequences | Participation by people who are not whales or the team | DAOs, protocols with live treasuries |

Pick one or two. A community asked to do all five does none of them well.

The evidence for the measures varies by job. For teaching, Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities (vendor research) found that, outside GitHub, members replied to each other 28% of the time against 13% for company staff. When the job is teaching, the share of questions members answer is the number to move, and it is measurable on most platforms.

For governing, the measure has to exclude the people who would decide anyway. A 2024 study of Aave, Compound, Lido and Uniswap governance found that on a typical proposal only about 5% of tokens were cast, and that the top three or four holders could decide almost every vote. Governance participation that counts only the largest wallets measures concentration, not community.

> Silence is the correct response to no job. A community with nothing to do will do nothing, however many people are in it.

## Web3 and AI, differently

**Web3 communities** are often holders first and users second. That is fine if you give holders a reason to become users: early access, a role in testing new markets, recognition in the product. It goes wrong when the only shared interest is price, because price is the one thing the team cannot promise. Our piece on [community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) covers how to design for the holders who stay.

**AI communities** are usually users or developers. The job is often *test* and *teach*: power users find failure cases faster than your QA, and their prompt tricks become your best onboarding content. Treat them as an extension of the product team.

## Designing for the job

**Channel:** pick the place where the job gets done. Testing happens in a structured feedback channel or a private group, not a 10,000-person server. Common Room found engagement rates of 2% to 12% across surfaces, highest in smaller communities.

**Rituals:** a weekly office hour, a monthly build review, a release preview. Rhythm beats announcements.

**Recognition:** name contributors publicly and specifically. In web3, onchain credentials or roles can make this portable; in AI, changelog credits and early feature access work well. Nielsen's advice from 2006 still holds: reward contributors, but not so heavily that the most active few crowd out everyone else.

**Ownership:** the community lives in channels where you control the records, so it survives a platform policy change.

Treat the community's output the way you treat any other content: with a named reader and a job. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) sets out the same discipline for marketing content.

Illustrative example: changing the job and the measure

Decision
:   A developer-tools company stopped reporting Discord member count to its board and started reporting the share of support questions answered by members within 24 hours.

Reason and owner
:   The server had grown fourfold in a year while support tickets also rose. The head of community owned the change, with the support lead.

What changed
:   The team created one help channel, credited answerers in the changelog and moved repeated answers into documentation. Member-answered questions became the number reviewed each month.

Illustrative: a composite of patterns across early-stage technical products, not a single company.

## The checklist

| Check | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| One or two named jobs | Written down and agreed by the founder |
| A contribution metric for each job | Reported monthly in place of member count |
| No paid-for posting | No growth tactic depends on paying for posts |
| A weekly ritual | On the calendar and moving the job forward |
| Named recognition | Contributors credited by name in the product or changelog |
| Owned records | Member list and contribution log held outside any single platform |

## lowob takeaways

- **Count contribution, not people.** Member counts are easy to buy, easy to inflate with incentives and nearly impossible for outsiders to verify.
- **Pick one or two jobs.** The five community jobs are test, teach, refer, build and govern.
- **Expect inequality.** A small minority will do most of the work, so design for them and measure them.
- **Own the record.** Keep the community in channels whose records you control so it survives a platform policy change.

## Common questions

### How should a startup measure community success?

Measure contribution to a defined job, not size. Depending on the job, that means bugs found, questions answered by members, referred sign-ups, integrations shipped, or governance participation by people who are not whales or the team.

### Why is community member count a bad metric?

Member counts are easy to inflate and impossible to verify, and they hide participation inequality: in one study of four networks, the top 1% of members wrote about 75% of posts. Growth in members is mostly growth in readers.

### What are the risks of incentive-driven community growth?

It selects for people who want the reward and depends on platforms you do not control. When X revoked API access for pay-to-post apps in January 2026, those programmes shut down and the KAITO token fell sharply.

### What is the 90-9-1 rule in online communities?

It is Jakob Nielsen's observation that about 90% of members read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. Studies since have found similar patterns, so plan for a small core.

## Sources and notes

- [CMX, 2025 Community Industry Report](https://start.bevy.com/hubfs/2025%20CMX%20Community%20Industry%20Report-1.pdf?hsLang=en), 2025. Survey of 589 community professionals, May to June 2025; CMX is owned by Bevy, a community software vendor; self-reported.
- [Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/), 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; the ratios are a rule of thumb, not a measured constant.
- [van Mierlo, The 1% Rule in Four Digital Health Social Networks, Journal of Medical Internet Research](https://www.jmir.org/2014/2/e33/), 4 February 2014. Peer-reviewed observational study of 63,990 members; health networks, not commercial communities.
- [The Block, Kaito token plummets after X revises API policies to ban InfoFi crypto projects](https://www.theblock.co/post/385805/kaito-token-plummets-x-revises-api-policies-ban-infofi-crypto-projects), 15 January 2026. News report; price moves are intraday.
- [Falk, Pathan, Rigas and Tsoukalas, Blockchain Governance: An Empirical Analysis of User Engagement on DAOs, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.10945v1), 15 July 2024. Preprint; four Ethereum DeFi protocols to December 2022.
- [Common Room, 360: Community-Led Growth Report](https://www.commonroom.io/blog/360-community-led-growth-report/), 17 November 2022. Vendor research on 141 communities using Common Room; 2022 data.
- The five-jobs table, checklist and example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.
